corpus_topic: Vitamin D supplementation and risk/treatment of acute respiratory infection (ARI)
selection_note: REVIEW1.docx's 20-paper literature survey (methods papers on NLP claim verification: SciFact, ContraCrow, NLI, etc.) was inspected first per the task instructions and found unsuitable as EXPERIMENT CONTENT: those papers are about claim-verification methods, not primary scientific findings, so they contain no comparable claims to match across documents. They remain the correct source for prior-art risk assessment (see the technical audit), not for this corpus. This manifest supplements REVIEW1 with real, freely-accessible primary/secondary research literature on one coherent topic, selected to contain genuine supporting, contradicting, neutral, and differing-population/evidence-strength cases.

papers.title: Vitamin D supplementation to prevent acute respiratory infections: systematic review and meta-analysis of stratified aggregate data
papers.authors: Jolliffe DA, Camargo CA Jr, Sluyter JD, et al. (Martineau AR, senior author)
papers.access_type: open access preprint, freely downloadable, full text retrieved directly in this session
papers.license: medRxiv preprint license (author/funder retains copyright; preprint displayed in perpetuity by medRxiv); not certified by peer review
papers.topic: Vitamin D and ARI prevention (updated meta-analysis of 46 RCTs, 64,086 participants)
papers.reason_for_selection: Largest, most recent aggregate-data meta-analysis on the topic; reports both a null overall effect and statistically significant protective subgroup effects (children aged 1.00-15.99y, daily dosing, 400-1000 IU/day, trials <=12 months), giving genuine within-paper heterogeneity useful for entity/relation-alignment stress-testing.
key_reported_findings: Overall: vitamin D vs placebo did not significantly reduce ARI risk (OR 0.94, 95% CI 0.88-1.00, 40 studies, 61,589 participants).
Subgroup, ages 1.00-15.99 years: statistically significant protective effect (OR 0.74, 95% CI 0.60-0.92, 16 studies).
Subgroup, daily dosing: statistically significant protective effect (OR 0.84, 95% CI 0.73-0.97).
Subgroup, 400-1000 IU/day daily dose: statistically significant protective effect (OR 0.70, 95% CI 0.55-0.89).

papers.title: Vitamin D and acute respiratory infection: secondary analysis of a previous randomised controlled trial and updated meta-analyses
papers.authors: Bolland MJ, Avenell A, Grey A, Gamble G
papers.access_type: open access preprint, freely downloadable, full text retrieved directly in this session
papers.topic: Methodological critique/reanalysis of the Blue Sky (Mongolia schoolchildren) trial underlying earlier positive meta-analyses
papers.reason_for_selection: Explicit, real methodological contradiction of the subgroup finding used to support 'vitamin D protects children with low baseline status' claims in earlier meta-analyses (predecessors of P1's 2021 version); once properly adjusted for cluster-randomisation, the same underlying trial data show no significant effect. This is a genuine same-topic, opposing-conclusion pair grounded in a documented scientific dispute, not a constructed example.
key_reported_findings: After adjusting for cluster-randomisation design, vitamin D supplementation showed no statistically significant effect on ARI risk in any treatment group of the Blue Sky trial, or pooled (OR 0.58, 95% CI 0.26-1.29).
Updated meta-analysis incorporating the corrected cluster-adjusted data: OR 0.94 (95% CI 0.88-1.01), no significant protective effect.
Explicitly disputes the earlier meta-analyses' reliance on Blue Sky trial data analysed as if individually randomised.

papers.title: Vitamin D Supplements for Prevention of COVID-19 or other Acute Respiratory Infections: a Phase 3 Randomised Controlled Trial (CORONAVIT)
papers.authors: Jolliffe DA, Holt H, Greenig M, et al. (Martineau AR, senior author)
papers.access_type: open access preprint, freely downloadable, full text retrieved directly in this session
papers.topic: Vitamin D 'test-and-treat' for ARI and COVID-19 prevention in UK adults (single large RCT, n=6200)
papers.reason_for_selection: A single large, well-powered RCT (not a meta-analysis) in a distinct population (general UK adults, high baseline sub-optimal vitamin D prevalence) and a distinct intervention design (test-and-treat, 800 vs 3200 IU/day) from P1/P2, reporting a clean null result. Provides a different evidence-strength/design profile (single RCT vs meta-analyses) for the same overall question.
key_reported_findings: No statistically significant reduction in all-cause ARI: higher-dose vs no-offer OR 1.09 (95% CI 0.82-1.46); lower-dose vs no-offer OR 1.26 (95% CI 0.96-1.66).
No statistically significant reduction in COVID-19: higher-dose vs no-offer OR 1.13 (95% CI 0.78-1.63); lower-dose vs no-offer OR 1.39 (95% CI 0.98-1.97).
Vitamin D supplementation was safe and raised serum 25(OH)D but did not protect against ARI or COVID-19 in this population.

papers.title: Efficacy of Vitamin D Supplements in Treatment of Acute Respiratory Infection: A Meta-analysis for Randomized Controlled Trials
papers.authors: (PMC record; full author list not independently verified in this session)
papers.access_type: PARTIAL — open-access PMC record confirmed (PMCID PMC8955452, free full text per PMC policy); this session could only retrieve the indexed abstract/results text via web search, because direct retrieval of the PMC article page was blocked by an automated bot-check (reCAPTCHA interstitial) in this sandbox. Full text was NOT independently fetched in this session.
papers.license: Per PMC open-access subset (specific journal license not verified in this session)
papers.topic: Vitamin D and ARI TREATMENT (as opposed to prevention) - meta-analysis of 18 RCTs, 3648 participants
papers.reason_for_selection: Only treatment-focused (vs. prevention-focused) meta-analysis identified for this corpus, giving a distinct claim type ('vitamin D helps treat an existing ARI') to compare against the prevention claims in P1-P3, P5.
key_reported_findings: Meta-analysis of 18 RCTs found a statistically significant beneficial effect of vitamin D in treatment of ARI (RR 1.07, 95% CI 1.01-1.13, I2=66.9%).
NOTE: this finding is taken from indexed abstract text only; the full paper (methods, risk-of-bias detail) was not independently reviewed in this session.

papers.title: The role of vitamin D in the prevention and treatment of acute respiratory infections in pediatric populations: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
papers.authors: (PMC record; full author list not independently verified in this session)
papers.access_type: PARTIAL — same limitation as P4: open-access PMC record confirmed, but this session's automated fetch was blocked by a bot-check interstitial; only the indexed abstract text was retrieved via web search.
papers.license: Per PMC open-access subset (specific journal license not verified in this session)
papers.topic: Vitamin D and ARI in pediatric populations specifically (prevention AND treatment combined), 17 RCTs, 18,372 participants
papers.reason_for_selection: Directly comparable population (pediatric) to P1's statistically significant child subgroup finding, but reaches the opposite overall conclusion for children as a population - a genuine same-population, differing-conclusion pair (though P1's subgroup is prevention-only, daily-dosing-only, while P5 pools prevention and treatment trials, which is itself a relevant condition difference for entity/relation alignment testing).
key_reported_findings: Vitamin D supplementation did NOT significantly reduce pediatric ARI incidence (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.64-1.06), hospitalisation duration, recovery time, or all-cause mortality.
NOTE: taken from indexed abstract text only; full paper not independently reviewed in this session.

papers_rejected_from_review1.note: All 20 papers in REVIEW1.docx's literature survey were reviewed. None were selected for the experimental corpus.
papers_rejected_from_review1.reason: REVIEW1's papers (SciFact, SciFact-Open, SCITAB, Clinical Contradiction Detection, ContraCrow/PaperQA2, Sentence-BERT, etc.) are methods/systems papers ABOUT claim verification, contradiction detection, or NLI - they do not themselves contain comparable scientific findings-claims (e.g. 'X reduces Y') that could be extracted and cross-document-matched by AERF Engine. Using them as pipeline input would mean extracting claims like 'SciFact contains 1.4K claims' rather than substantive scientific findings, which would not exercise cross-document support/contradiction reasoning meaningfully. They remain correctly used elsewhere (technical audit, prior-art risk section) as prior art on the claim-verification METHODS themselves, which is a different role from experimental CONTENT.
